messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 69
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Nanny
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Care: Seeking medical or psychological help, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

When Minh Tran talks about the year his wife died and his grandson became critically ill, the sequence breaks apart on him. He knows the illness came after the funeral, and he knows there was an ambulance, a hospital room, and a night when he was told the boy might not survive, but when he tries to put it in order the memories do not line up into a clear story. Instead they come at him as sharp pieces: the bluish color around the child’s mouth, the rush of feet in a hallway, a monitor sounding, a doctor’s face moving while Minh could not take in the words. Those moments do not feel old to him. They arrive with a force that makes ordinary memory seem pale by comparison, as if what happened in the hospital is more real than the room he is sitting in now. At times he is suddenly certain, for a few seconds, that he is back there and that the child is again on the edge of dying.

Minh is a 69-year-old widowed Vietnamese American man who has worked for years as a nanny, caring for young children in other people’s homes. He had always seen himself as patient, reliable, and calm with children, someone who knew how to steady a room when a child was upset. During his grandson’s illness, that sense of himself was badly shaken. What frightened him most was not only that a child he loved might die, but that he stood in the hospital unable to do anything useful. He remembers trying to read the adults around him—the doctors, the nurses, even extended family members—and coming away with the sense that no one was saying everything plainly. Since then he has come to believe that people are not what they seem, that reassurance often hides something worse, and that he can no longer trust appearances.

In the months after the medical crisis, Minh did not find that the experience settled into the past. He tried very hard not to think about it. If an image of the hospital intruded, he would immediately turn to something else: wiping kitchen counters again, reorganizing a diaper bag, folding children’s laundry that was already folded. He kept his mind occupied as constantly as he could. Silence felt dangerous. At home, after his shift ended, he left the television on for company and distraction even when he was not really watching it. When thoughts of that night pushed in anyway, he would force himself to think of grocery lists, bus schedules, recipes, anything neutral and practical enough to crowd the memory out.

His work as a nanny brings him into exactly the kind of moments he now struggles with. When one of the children in his care gets a fever, coughs hard, or seems listless on the couch, he feels his body tense before he has fully registered why. He becomes intensely alert to any sign that a child is “not right.” If a parent says, “He’s probably fine,” Minh finds himself silently doubting them. He watches for changes in breathing, skin color, appetite, energy. In those moments the hospital memory can hit with such immediacy that he feels briefly transported, as though the danger is happening again in front of him. He does not explain this to the families he works for. Instead, he keeps moving, tidying, checking supplies, finding tasks to do with his hands.

Although he spends his life caring for children, Minh avoids medical care for himself and has also avoided psychological help. He cannot bear the idea of sitting in a clinic waiting room or being asked detailed questions that might pull the hospital scenes into focus. Seeking help feels too close to the world in which the worst happened. Over time this avoidance has narrowed his life. He still works, but he no longer feels like the man he used to be. He says, in effect, that the person he has become is unrecognizable to him: suspicious, preoccupied, never fully at ease. He has come to believe that something in him was permanently altered for the worse during his grandson’s illness and never came back.

Those changes have also affected his relationships. Since being widowed, much of his emotional connection has come through family and the children he cares for, yet he has grown more guarded with both. He does not easily accept comfort. If someone tells him not to worry, he hears distance rather than kindness. He keeps the worst parts of his experience to himself partly because he cannot tell it cleanly and partly because he expects other people will not really understand or will conceal their true reactions.

What finally brought Minh to seek help was not a new trauma but the recognition that he could no longer manage the strain by staying busy. Recently, while caring for a child with a high fever, he was overcome by the sense that he was back in the hospital again, and afterward he could not shake the feeling that he was living inside that old night. It frightened him that he still had so little control over where his mind went. He has come in now because he wants some way to live with children’s ordinary illnesses without being pulled into that same terror, but he is also afraid that talking about what happened will make it feel even more immediate than it already does.
